A decrease in supply at every price
A movement along the existing supply curve only
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: A decrease in supply at every price

The Theory of Supply.text: An improvement in production technology that lowers production costs will typically cause
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: An increase in supply

The Theory of Supply.text: The imposition of a sales tax on a commodity will most likely cause
options: An increase in supply at every price
No effect on the position of the supply curve
A decrease in supply at every price
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: A decrease in supply at every price

The Theory of Supply.text: The grant of a government subsidy to producers of a commodity will most likely cause
options: A decrease in the number of sellers
No change in the supply curve
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: An increase in supply

The Theory of Supply.text: An increase in the number of firms producing and selling a commodity will, other things being equal, cause
options: Market supply to remain the same
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: Market supply to increase

The Theory of Supply.text: For agricultural commodities, which of the following is a particularly important determinant of supply?
options: The exchange rate of a foreign currency unrelated to the crop
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: Weather and climatic conditions

The Theory of Supply.text: A supply schedule is best described as
options: A table showing the price consumers are willing to pay for various quantities
A record of a firm's fixed costs
A graph showing consumer income levels
A table showing the various quantities of a commodity that sellers are willing to offer at different prices
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: A table showing the various quantities of a commodity that sellers are willing to offer at different prices

The Theory of Supply.text: When plotted with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, a normal supply curve slopes
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: Upward from left to right

The Theory of Supply.text: The law of supply states that, other things being equal,
options: The higher the price of a commodity, the lower the quantity supplied
The lower the price, the higher the quantity supplied
Price has no effect on quantity supplied
The higher the price of a commodity, the higher the quantity supplied
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: The higher the price of a commodity, the higher the quantity supplied

The Theory of Supply.text: The main reason supply curves typically slope upward is that
options: Higher prices provide greater incentive and cover rising marginal costs of producing more output
Consumers demand more at higher prices
Government always subsidises production at high prices
Firms prefer to sell less as prices rise
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: Higher prices provide greater incentive and cover rising marginal costs of producing more output

The Theory of Supply.text: A change in the quantity supplied of a good, caused solely by a change in its own price, is shown on a diagram as
options: A shift of the whole supply curve
A change in the axis scale
A rotation of the demand curve
A movement along the same supply curve
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: A movement along the same supply curve

The Theory of Supply.text: A change in supply, as distinct from a change in quantity supplied, occurs when
options: The price of the commodity itself changes
There is a movement along the existing curve
A non-price factor such as cost of production or technology changes, shifting the whole curve
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: A non-price factor such as cost of production or technology changes, shifting the whole curve

The Theory of Supply.text: An increase in supply is represented graphically by
options: A rightward shift of the supply curve
A leftward shift of the supply curve
An upward movement along the supply curve
A downward movement along the supply curve
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: A rightward shift of the supply curve

The Theory of Supply.text: A decrease in supply, perhaps due to a rise in input costs, is represented graphically by
options: A rightward shift of the supply curve
A movement down the existing curve
A leftward shift of the supply curve
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: A leftward shift of the supply curve

The Theory of Supply.text: Joint supply (or complementary supply) occurs when
options: A single production process yields two or more products together, such as beef and hides from cattle
Several firms compete to sell the same product
A resource can be used to produce several different alternative goods
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: A single production process yields two or more products together, such as beef and hides from cattle

The Theory of Supply.text: If the price of beef rises, leading producers to slaughter more cattle, the supply of hides (a by-product) is likely to
options: Fall, since hides and beef are substitutes
Rise, because beef and hides are in joint supply
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: Rise, because beef and hides are in joint supply

The Theory of Supply.text: Competitive supply refers to a situation where
options: A single resource or land can be used to produce alternative goods, so that producing more of one means producing less of another
Two goods are always produced together in fixed proportions
Supply is fixed regardless of price
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: A single resource or land can be used to produce alternative goods, so that producing more of one means producing less of another

The Theory of Supply.text: A farmer who can use the same piece of land to grow either maize or cassava, but not both at once, faces a situation of
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: Competitive supply

The Theory of Supply.text: Composite supply exists when
options: A commodity can be supplied from two or more different sources to meet a single demand, such as sugar from cane and sugar from beet
One production process yields two goods together
A single resource has alternative uses
Goods are supplied only in fixed quantities
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: A commodity can be supplied from two or more different sources to meet a single demand, such as sugar from cane and sugar from beet

The Theory of Supply.text: Electricity generated from hydro sources and electricity generated from thermal (gas) sources, both feeding the same national grid, best illustrates
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: Composite supply

The Theory of Supply.text: Price elasticity of supply measures
options: The responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in the price of the commodity
The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price
The responsiveness of income to a change in supply
The change in total cost as output changes
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: The responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in the price of the commodity

The Theory of Supply.text: Supply is said to be elastic when
options: The percentage change in quantity supplied is less than the percentage change in price
Quantity supplied does not change at all with price
The percentage change in quantity supplied is greater than the percentage change in price
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: The percentage change in quantity supplied is greater than the percentage change in price

The Theory of Supply.text: Supply is said to be inelastic when
options: The percentage change in quantity supplied is less than the percentage change in price
The percentage change in quantity supplied is greater than the percentage change in price
The percentage change in quantity supplied equals the percentage change in price
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: The percentage change in quantity supplied is less than the percentage change in price

The Theory of Supply.text: A vertical supply curve represents supply that is
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: Perfectly inelastic

The Theory of Supply.text: A horizontal supply curve represents supply that is
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: Perfectly elastic

The Theory of Supply.text: A straight-line supply curve that passes through the origin has an elasticity of supply equal to
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: 1 at every point

The Theory of Supply.text: The price of a good rises from ₦40 to ₦50 (a 25% increase), and quantity supplied rises from 200 to 250 units (a 25% increase). The price elasticity of supply is
The price of a commodity rises from ₦100 to ₦120 (a 20% increase), causing quantity supplied to rise from 500 to 600 units (a 20% increase). Supply in this case is
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: Unitary elastic

The Theory of Supply.text: The price of yams rises from ₦500 to ₦600 (a 20% increase), and quantity supplied rises from 1,000 to 1,080 tubers (an 8% increase). The price elasticity of supply (approximately) is
Following from the previous question, since the elasticity coefficient is less than 1, supply of yams in that price range is
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: Inelastic

The Theory of Supply.text: The price of fish rises by 10%, causing quantity supplied to rise by 30%. The price elasticity of supply is
Which of the following is a key determinant of the price elasticity of supply of a commodity?
options: The consumer's taste for the good
The length of time producers have to adjust output
The price of a completely unrelated good
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: The length of time producers have to adjust output

The Theory of Supply.text: Supply tends to be more elastic when
options: Producers have limited spare production capacity
Goods are perishable and cannot be stored
Producers can easily store the commodity and have spare capacity to increase output
There is only one producer in the market
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: Producers can easily store the commodity and have spare capacity to increase output

The Theory of Supply.text: The supply of perishable goods such as fresh tomatoes, immediately after harvest, tends to be
options: Relatively inelastic in the very short run
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: Relatively inelastic in the very short run

The Theory of Supply.text: Which time period, as classified in supply analysis, allows producers the greatest scope to vary all factors of production, thereby making supply most elastic?
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: The long run

The Theory of Supply.text: In the 'momentary' or market period, supply of a good is often described as
options: Perfectly inelastic, since output cannot be changed instantly
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: Perfectly inelastic, since output cannot be changed instantly

The Theory of Supply.text: Ease of factor mobility (how easily labour and capital can move into an industry) affects supply elasticity because
options: It has no bearing on how quickly output can be expanded
Greater mobility of factors allows faster expansion of output in response to price changes, raising elasticity
It only affects demand, not supply
It reduces the number of firms in the industry
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: Greater mobility of factors allows faster expansion of output in response to price changes, raising elasticity

The Theory of Supply.text: Knowledge of the price elasticity of supply is useful to policymakers mainly because it helps predict
options: How consumer taste will change over time
How quickly producers will respond to price changes, useful for taxation and price control decisions
The exact colour preferences of consumers
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: How quickly producers will respond to price changes, useful for taxation and price control decisions

The Theory of Supply.text: Which of the following would most likely cause a leftward shift of the supply curve for a manufactured good?
options: A fall in the price of raw materials
A rise in wages paid to workers with no offsetting productivity gain
An increase in the number of firms in the industry
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: A rise in wages paid to workers with no offsetting productivity gain

The Theory of Supply.text: If the government removes an existing subsidy on fertiliser, the supply curve for farm produce that depends on fertiliser will most likely
options: Remain in exactly the same position
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: Shift to the left

The Theory of Supply.text: Producers' expectations of a future price rise for a storable commodity will most likely cause them to
options: Increase current supply to sell before the price rises
Withhold some current supply, reducing quantity offered now, in order to sell later at a higher price
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: Withhold some current supply, reducing quantity offered now, in order to sell later at a higher price

The Theory of Supply.text: Which of the following best distinguishes a movement along the supply curve from a shift of the supply curve?
options: Both are caused only by changes in the price of the good
A movement is caused by a price change of the good itself, while a shift is caused by changes in non-price determinants such as cost or technology
A shift is caused by a price change, while a movement is caused by non-price factors
There is no real difference between the two concepts
The Theory of Supply.correct_answer: A movement is caused by a price change of the good itself, while a shift is caused by changes in non-price determinants such as cost or technology

The Theory of Price Determination.text: In economics, what is a market?
options: Any place, arrangement, or means by which buyers and sellers of a commodity are brought into contact to exchange goods and services
A physical building where goods are displayed for sale only
A government agency that fixes prices for all goods
A warehouse where unsold goods are stored
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: Any place, arrangement, or means by which buyers and sellers of a commodity are brought into contact to exchange goods and services

The Theory of Price Determination.text: Equilibrium price is best defined as the price at which:
options: the government fixes the price of a commodity
quantity demanded of a commodity equals quantity supplied
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: quantity demanded of a commodity equals quantity supplied

The Theory of Price Determination.text: One major function of the price mechanism is to ration scarce goods among consumers. This means that:
options: government agencies decide who receives goods
price allocates the limited quantity of a good to those willing and able to pay the market price
all consumers receive equal quantities regardless of price
goods are shared free of charge to everyone
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: price allocates the limited quantity of a good to those willing and able to pay the market price

The Theory of Price Determination.text: The price mechanism allocates resources among competing uses mainly by:
options: instructing producers on what to produce through government directives
directing resources towards production of goods that are more profitable and in higher demand
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: directing resources towards production of goods that are more profitable and in higher demand

The Theory of Price Determination.text: When quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the current price (excess demand), the price will tend to:
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: rise until equilibrium is restored

The Theory of Price Determination.text: When quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at the current price (excess supply), the price will tend to:
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: fall until equilibrium is restored

The Theory of Price Determination.text: Equilibrium quantity in a market is achieved when:
options: quantity demanded equals quantity supplied at the prevailing price
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: quantity demanded equals quantity supplied at the prevailing price

The Theory of Price Determination.text: A minimum price (price floor) is:
options: a price set below the equilibrium price by government
the lowest price a consumer is willing to pay
a price fixed by government or an authority above the equilibrium price to protect sellers
the price at which a firm makes zero profit
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: a price fixed by government or an authority above the equilibrium price to protect sellers

The Theory of Price Determination.text: A maximum price (price ceiling) is:
options: a price fixed by government below the equilibrium price to protect buyers
a price fixed above the equilibrium price to protect sellers
the highest price a firm can charge without government interference
the price at which supply equals zero
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: a price fixed by government below the equilibrium price to protect buyers

The Theory of Price Determination.text: If government imposes a minimum wage above the equilibrium wage rate in the labour market, the likely result is:
options: a surplus of labour, that is, unemployment
wages will automatically fall back to equilibrium
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: a surplus of labour, that is, unemployment

The Theory of Price Determination.text: Rent control, which fixes rent below the equilibrium rent in the housing market, is likely to lead to:
options: a shortage of houses for rent
an immediate increase in housing supply
no change in the housing market
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: a shortage of houses for rent

The Theory of Price Determination.text: In the factor market for labour, the wage rate is determined by:
options: the cost of production of goods only
the interaction of demand for and supply of labour
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: the interaction of demand for and supply of labour

The Theory of Price Determination.text: If demand for a commodity increases while supply remains unchanged, the equilibrium price and quantity will:
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: both rise

The Theory of Price Determination.text: If demand for a commodity decreases while supply remains unchanged, the equilibrium price and quantity will:
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: both fall

The Theory of Price Determination.text: If supply of a commodity increases while demand remains unchanged, the equilibrium price and quantity will:
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: price falls, quantity rises

The Theory of Price Determination.text: If supply of a commodity decreases while demand remains unchanged, the equilibrium price and quantity will:
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: price rises, quantity falls

The Theory of Price Determination.text: If both demand and supply increase by the same proportion, the equilibrium quantity will:
options: rise, while the effect on price is indeterminate without further information
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: rise, while the effect on price is indeterminate without further information

The Theory of Price Determination.text: If both demand and supply decrease, the equilibrium quantity will:
options: fall, while the effect on price is indeterminate without further information
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: fall, while the effect on price is indeterminate without further information

The Theory of Price Determination.text: If demand increases and supply decreases at the same time, equilibrium price will:
options: fall, with the quantity effect indeterminate
rise, while the effect on quantity is indeterminate without further information
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: rise, while the effect on quantity is indeterminate without further information

The Theory of Price Determination.text: If demand decreases and supply increases at the same time, equilibrium price will:
options: fall, while the effect on quantity is indeterminate without further information
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: fall, while the effect on quantity is indeterminate without further information

The Theory of Price Determination.text: On a demand and supply diagram, if price is set above the equilibrium price, the gap between quantity supplied and quantity demanded at that price represents:
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: a surplus

The Theory of Price Determination.text: On a demand and supply diagram, if price is set below the equilibrium price, the gap between quantity demanded and quantity supplied represents:
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: a shortage

The Theory of Price Determination.text: The price system performs a signalling function by:
options: preventing entry of new firms into an industry
informing producers, through price changes, of changes in consumers' wants so that resources can be reallocated
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: informing producers, through price changes, of changes in consumers' wants so that resources can be reallocated

The Theory of Price Determination.text: Besides rationing and signalling, another important function of the price mechanism is the ___ function, which channels resources into the production of goods that are most profitable.
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: allocative

The Theory of Price Determination.text: A government most commonly imposes price control on essential commodities in order to:
options: protect consumers from being exploited through excessively high prices
increase the profit of monopolist producers
eliminate the need for a market altogether
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: protect consumers from being exploited through excessively high prices

The Theory of Price Determination.text: A price floor is commonly used by government in agricultural markets mainly to:
options: guarantee farmers a minimum income by preventing prices from falling too low
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: guarantee farmers a minimum income by preventing prices from falling too low

The Theory of Price Determination.text: A common consequence of an effective price ceiling with persistent excess demand is the emergence of:
options: a general fall in production costs
a black market where goods are sold illegally above the fixed price
an automatic increase in the legal supply
a permanent surplus of the good
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: a black market where goods are sold illegally above the fixed price

The Theory of Price Determination.text: Under a price floor scheme for an agricultural product, when a surplus occurs at the fixed minimum price, government typically:
options: allows the price to fall to equilibrium
bans the sale of the product
buys up the surplus output to maintain the price, often called a buffer stock or support-buying scheme
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: buys up the surplus output to maintain the price, often called a buffer stock or support-buying scheme

The Theory of Price Determination.text: In factor markets, the price paid for the use of capital is called:
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: interest

The Theory of Price Determination.text: In factor markets, the price paid for the use of land is called:
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: rent

The Theory of Price Determination.text: In factor markets, the reward paid to the entrepreneur for bearing risk and organising production is called:
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: profit

The Theory of Price Determination.text: In factor markets, the price paid for the services of labour is called:
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: wages

The Theory of Price Determination.text: At a price of N50, quantity demanded of a good is 100 units and quantity supplied is 60 units. At a price of N70, quantity demanded is 60 units and quantity supplied is 100 units. Assuming both relationships are linear, what is the equilibrium price and quantity?
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: N60 and 80 units

The Theory of Price Determination.text: At the equilibrium price of N40, both quantity demanded and quantity supplied equal 200 units. Government then imposes a price ceiling of N30, at which quantity demanded rises to 260 units and quantity supplied falls to 150 units. What is the size of the resulting shortage?
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: 110 units

The Theory of Price Determination.text: A situation in which quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the ruling price is also known as:
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: a shortage or excess demand

The Theory of Price Determination.text: A situation in which quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at the ruling price is also known as:
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: a surplus or glut

The Theory of Price Determination.text: Which of the following best describes the likely effect of setting a minimum wage significantly above the equilibrium wage in a competitive labour market?
options: It creates unemployment because quantity of labour supplied exceeds quantity demanded
It has no effect on employment
It automatically lowers the equilibrium wage
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: It creates unemployment because quantity of labour supplied exceeds quantity demanded

The Theory of Price Determination.text: Black markets tend to develop specifically as a response to:
options: an effective price ceiling that creates persistent excess demand
an effective price floor that creates persistent excess supply
perfectly free market pricing with no controls
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: an effective price ceiling that creates persistent excess demand

The Theory of Price Determination.text: Government purchase and storage of surplus produce (a buffer stock scheme) is a typical response to:
options: an effective price floor that generates a persistent surplus
a fall in consumer demand only
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: an effective price floor that generates a persistent surplus

The Theory of Price Determination.text: The idea that individuals pursuing their own self-interest in a free market unintentionally promote the general good through the price mechanism, without central direction, was famously described by Adam Smith as:
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: the invisible hand

The Theory of Price Determination.text: Market price differs from equilibrium (normal) price mainly because market price:
options: can fluctuate in the short run due to temporary changes in demand or supply before settling at equilibrium
is unrelated to demand and supply
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: can fluctuate in the short run due to temporary changes in demand or supply before settling at equilibrium

The Theory of Price Determination.text: A factor market is a market in which:
options: only finished consumer goods are bought and sold
factors of production such as land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship are bought and sold
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: factors of production such as land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship are bought and sold

The Theory of Price Determination.text: A product market (goods market) is a market in which:
options: factors of production are exchanged for use in production
finished goods and services are bought and sold by households and firms
only money is exchanged for money
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: finished goods and services are bought and sold by households and firms

The Theory of Price Determination.text: If, on a demand and supply diagram, both the demand curve and the supply curve shift to the right by the same horizontal distance, the equilibrium quantity will increase while equilibrium price will:
options: remain unchanged, since both curves have shifted by the same amount
The Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: remain unchanged, since both curves have shifted by the same amount

The Theory of Production.text: Which of the following best defines production in economics?
options: The buying and selling of finished goods only
The creation or addition of utility (value) to goods and services to satisfy human wants
The storage of goods until they are needed
The distribution of income among factors of production
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: The creation or addition of utility (value) to goods and services to satisfy human wants

The Theory of Production.text: Primary production refers to:
options: the processing of raw materials into finished goods
the provision of services such as banking and transport
the extraction of raw materials directly from land, sea or nature, such as farming, fishing, mining and forestry
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: the extraction of raw materials directly from land, sea or nature, such as farming, fishing, mining and forestry

The Theory of Production.text: Secondary production involves:
options: the processing or manufacturing of raw materials obtained from primary production into semi-finished or finished goods
the direct extraction of natural resources
the provision of commercial services like insurance
the distribution of goods to final consumers only
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: the processing or manufacturing of raw materials obtained from primary production into semi-finished or finished goods

The Theory of Production.text: Tertiary production refers to:
options: the provision of services, such as banking, transport, education and health, that support primary and secondary production
the manufacture of machinery from raw materials
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: the provision of services, such as banking, transport, education and health, that support primary and secondary production

The Theory of Production.text: Total product (TP) is best described as:
options: the output produced by the last unit of a variable factor employed
output per unit of the variable factor employed
the cost incurred in producing one more unit of output
the total quantity of output produced by a given quantity of factors of production over a period of time
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: the total quantity of output produced by a given quantity of factors of production over a period of time

The Theory of Production.text: Average product (AP) is calculated as:
options: total product multiplied by the number of variable factors
total product divided by the quantity of the variable factor employed
the change in total product divided by the change in price
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: total product divided by the quantity of the variable factor employed

The Theory of Production.text: Marginal product (MP) refers to:
options: total product divided by total factors employed
the average output of all workers employed
the additional output resulting from employing one more unit of a variable factor, other factors held constant
the total revenue earned from selling one more unit
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: the additional output resulting from employing one more unit of a variable factor, other factors held constant

The Theory of Production.text: The law of variable proportions (law of diminishing returns) states that as more units of a variable factor are added to a fixed factor, other things being equal:
options: the marginal product of the variable factor will eventually decline
total product will fall continuously from the first unit
average product will always rise indefinitely
output will remain constant regardless of input added
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: the marginal product of the variable factor will eventually decline

The Theory of Production.text: In the stages of production under the law of variable proportions, Stage I is characterised by:
options: increasing marginal and average product as more variable factor is added
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: increasing marginal and average product as more variable factor is added

The Theory of Production.text: In Stage III of the law of variable proportions, which of the following occurs?
options: average product is at its maximum and rising
total product is rising at an increasing rate
marginal product becomes negative and total product begins to fall
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: marginal product becomes negative and total product begins to fall

The Theory of Production.text: A rational producer would normally choose to operate in which stage of production described by the law of variable proportions?
options: Stage II, where marginal product is positive but diminishing
Stage I, where marginal product is still rising
Stage III, where marginal product is negative
None of the stages, since output should always be zero
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: Stage II, where marginal product is positive but diminishing

The Theory of Production.text: Division of labour refers to:
options: sharing profits equally among all workers in a firm
dividing a firm's capital among shareholders
breaking down the production process into separate tasks, with each worker specialising in one task
rotating workers randomly between unrelated firms
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: breaking down the production process into separate tasks, with each worker specialising in one task

The Theory of Production.text: One major advantage of division of labour is that it:
options: requires every worker to be skilled in all tasks
increases the risk of structural unemployment only
increases efficiency and output through specialisation and increased skill of workers
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: increases efficiency and output through specialisation and increased skill of workers

The Theory of Production.text: A major disadvantage of excessive division of labour is that it may lead to:
options: higher output per worker in all cases
monotony and boredom for workers, reducing job satisfaction
lower dependence of workers on one another
an automatic increase in wages for all workers
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: monotony and boredom for workers, reducing job satisfaction

The Theory of Production.text: Division of labour tends to increase the interdependence of workers because:
options: each worker now produces a complete product alone
each worker depends on others who perform the other stages of production
it eliminates the need for coordination
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: each worker depends on others who perform the other stages of production

The Theory of Production.text: Internal economies of scale are cost advantages that a firm enjoys:
options: as a result of its own growth in size, independent of the growth of the industry
as a result of the growth of the whole industry in which it operates
only when government subsidises the firm
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: as a result of its own growth in size, independent of the growth of the industry

The Theory of Production.text: External economies of scale arise when:
options: a single firm expands its own plant size
the whole industry grows, benefiting all firms within it, for example through shared infrastructure or specialised suppliers
a firm reduces its output to cut cost
a firm merges with a foreign competitor only
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: the whole industry grows, benefiting all firms within it, for example through shared infrastructure or specialised suppliers

The Theory of Production.text: Which of the following is an example of an internal economy of scale?
options: Improved transport network built for the whole industry
A specialised labour pool developing in an industrial area
Growth of specialised component suppliers in a region
Bulk purchasing of raw materials at a discount due to a firm's own large scale of production
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: Bulk purchasing of raw materials at a discount due to a firm's own large scale of production

The Theory of Production.text: Internal diseconomies of scale occur when a firm grows so large that:
options: its average cost of production begins to rise due to problems such as poor coordination and management inefficiency
its average cost of production continues to fall indefinitely
it automatically becomes more efficient than smaller firms
government forces it to reduce output
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: its average cost of production begins to rise due to problems such as poor coordination and management inefficiency

The Theory of Production.text: External diseconomies of scale may result from the growth of an industry in a particular area, causing:
options: lower rents and land costs for all firms
congestion, higher local costs of inputs, and increased pollution affecting all firms in the area
an automatic increase in profit for every firm
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: congestion, higher local costs of inputs, and increased pollution affecting all firms in the area

The Theory of Production.text: A production function shows:
options: the total cost of producing a given output
the relationship between price and quantity demanded
the revenue earned from selling different quantities of output
the technical relationship between the quantities of inputs used and the maximum quantity of output that can be produced
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: the technical relationship between the quantities of inputs used and the maximum quantity of output that can be produced

The Theory of Production.text: Increasing returns to scale occur when a proportionate increase in all inputs leads to:
options: a less than proportionate increase in output
a more than proportionate increase in output
exactly the same proportionate increase in output
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: a more than proportionate increase in output

The Theory of Production.text: Constant returns to scale occur when a proportionate increase in all inputs leads to:
options: a more than proportionate increase in output
exactly the same proportionate increase in output
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: exactly the same proportionate increase in output

The Theory of Production.text: Decreasing returns to scale occur when a proportionate increase in all inputs leads to:
options: a less than proportionate increase in output
a more than proportionate increase in output
exactly the same proportionate change in output
output remaining fixed regardless of inputs
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: a less than proportionate increase in output

The Theory of Production.text: An isoquant is a curve that shows:
options: combinations of two goods that give a consumer equal satisfaction
different combinations of two factors of production that produce the same level of output
combinations of price and quantity that yield the same revenue
the total cost of production at various output levels
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: different combinations of two factors of production that produce the same level of output

The Theory of Production.text: An isocost line shows:
options: combinations of two goods yielding equal utility
combinations of output that cost the same to sell
the maximum output obtainable from fixed resources
all combinations of two factors of production that a firm can purchase for a given total cost, given factor prices
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: all combinations of two factors of production that a firm can purchase for a given total cost, given factor prices

The Theory of Production.text: A producer attains equilibrium (least-cost combination of inputs) at the point where:
options: the isoquant is tangent to the isocost line
the isoquant crosses the horizontal axis
the isocost line lies above all isoquants
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: the isoquant is tangent to the isocost line

The Theory of Production.text: If isoquants are convex to the origin, this reflects:
options: a constant marginal rate of technical substitution equal to zero
that the two factors of production are perfect substitutes at a fixed ratio
a diminishing marginal rate of technical substitution between the two factors
that output cannot be increased by adding more of either factor
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: a diminishing marginal rate of technical substitution between the two factors

The Theory of Production.text: Which of the following would most likely increase the productivity of labour in a firm?
options: A reduction in workers' training and skills
Improved technology, better training, and more efficient management
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: Improved technology, better training, and more efficient management

The Theory of Production.text: Which of the following is NOT typically classified as a type of production in the primary, secondary, tertiary classification?
options: Speculative production, referring to buying shares purely to resell at a higher price without adding any utility
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: Speculative production, referring to buying shares purely to resell at a higher price without adding any utility

The Theory of Production.text: The construction industry (building houses and roads) is generally classified under which type of production?
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: Secondary production

The Theory of Production.text: Which of the following best illustrates tertiary production?
options: A commercial bank providing loans and payment services to businesses
A factory assembling cars from parts
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: A commercial bank providing loans and payment services to businesses

The Theory of Production.text: As more workers are added to a fixed plot of farmland, output initially rises rapidly, then rises at a diminishing rate, and eventually falls. This pattern illustrates:
options: the law of variable proportions (diminishing returns)
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: the law of variable proportions (diminishing returns)

The Theory of Production.text: If total product is at its maximum, marginal product is:
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: equal to zero

The Theory of Production.text: When marginal product is greater than average product, average product must be:
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: rising

The Theory of Production.text: When marginal product is less than average product, average product must be:
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: falling

The Theory of Production.text: Which of the following is an example of an external economy of scale enjoyed by firms in an industrial cluster?
options: A firm's own improved managerial specialisation
A firm's own large-scale machinery reducing unit cost
The development of a skilled labour force and specialised suppliers in the local area, benefiting all firms
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: The development of a skilled labour force and specialised suppliers in the local area, benefiting all firms

The Theory of Production.text: Specialisation among nations or regions, similar to division of labour among workers, generally leads to:
options: reduced total output for the world
increased overall efficiency and output through concentration on what each does best
elimination of the need for trade
equal production of all goods by every country
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: increased overall efficiency and output through concentration on what each does best

The Theory of Production.text: A firm's production function exhibits diminishing marginal returns to a single variable factor when, holding other factors fixed, additional units of that factor:
options: have no effect on total product
eventually add less and less to total output
always cause total product to fall immediately
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: eventually add less and less to total output

The Theory of Production.text: Which of the following factors would most likely reduce labour productivity in a factory?
options: Frequent power outages and poor working conditions
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: Frequent power outages and poor working conditions

The Theory of Production.text: The marginal rate of technical substitution (MRTS) between two factors of production refers to:
options: the ratio of total cost to total output
the rate at which one factor can be substituted for another while keeping output constant
the change in price of one factor relative to another
the total output produced by two factors combined
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: the rate at which one factor can be substituted for another while keeping output constant

The Theory of Production.text: If a firm doubles all its inputs (labour and capital) and output more than doubles, the firm is experiencing:
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: increasing returns to scale

The Theory of Production.text: Which of the following best distinguishes 'returns to scale' from 'the law of variable proportions'?
options: Returns to scale considers changes in all factors of production together, while the law of variable proportions considers changes in one variable factor with others fixed
They are exactly the same concept with different names
Returns to scale applies only to agriculture while the law of variable proportions applies only to industry
Returns to scale applies only in the short run while variable proportions applies only in the long run
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: Returns to scale considers changes in all factors of production together, while the law of variable proportions considers changes in one variable factor with others fixed

The Theory of Production.text: In the long run, a firm can change:
options: none of its factors of production
only its variable factors, since all factors are fixed
all its factors of production, since there is no fixed factor in the long run
The Theory of Production.correct_answer: all its factors of production, since there is no fixed factor in the long run

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: Fixed cost (FC) is defined as:
options: cost that varies directly with output
the cost of raw materials used in production
cost that does not change with the level of output in the short run, such as rent on a factory building
the extra cost of producing one more unit
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: cost that does not change with the level of output in the short run, such as rent on a factory building

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: Variable cost (VC) is defined as:
options: cost that changes directly with the level of output, such as cost of raw materials and casual labour
cost that remains constant regardless of output
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: cost that changes directly with the level of output, such as cost of raw materials and casual labour

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: Total cost (TC) is calculated as:
options: the sum of total fixed cost and total variable cost
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: the sum of total fixed cost and total variable cost

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: Average cost (AC) is calculated as:
options: total cost divided by the quantity of output produced
total fixed cost divided by total variable cost
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: total cost divided by the quantity of output produced

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: Marginal cost (MC) is defined as:
options: the addition to total cost resulting from producing one more unit of output
the average cost of all units produced
total cost divided by total output
the fixed cost per unit of output
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: the addition to total cost resulting from producing one more unit of output

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: A firm produces 10 units at a total cost of N500 and 11 units at a total cost of N540. What is the marginal cost of the 11th unit?
If total fixed cost is N2,000 and total variable cost of producing 100 units is N3,000, what is the average cost per unit?
Total revenue (TR) is calculated as:
options: price per unit multiplied by the quantity of output sold
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: price per unit multiplied by the quantity of output sold

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: Average revenue (AR) is calculated as:
options: total revenue divided by the quantity of output sold, which equals price under perfect competition
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: total revenue divided by the quantity of output sold, which equals price under perfect competition

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: Marginal revenue (MR) is defined as:
options: the addition to total revenue resulting from selling one more unit of output
total revenue divided by average cost
the price of the first unit sold only
total revenue minus total variable cost
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: the addition to total revenue resulting from selling one more unit of output

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: A firm sells 20 units for a total revenue of N2,000 and 21 units for a total revenue of N2,080. What is the marginal revenue of the 21st unit?
If a firm sells 50 units of a good at N40 each, what is the total revenue and average revenue?
Under perfect competition, since the firm is a price taker, which of the following is true?
options: Price equals average revenue equals marginal revenue
Average revenue is always greater than price
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: Price equals average revenue equals marginal revenue

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: Explicit costs are:
options: costs that are never recorded by accountants
the opportunity cost of the entrepreneur's own time only
actual out-of-pocket payments a firm makes to outsiders for factors of production, such as wages, rent and raw material costs
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: actual out-of-pocket payments a firm makes to outsiders for factors of production, such as wages, rent and raw material costs

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: Implicit costs are:
options: payments made to workers employed by the firm
the opportunity cost of using resources owned by the firm itself, such as the entrepreneur's own capital or time, for which no direct cash payment is made
costs recorded in the firm's financial accounts as cash expenses
costs of raw materials purchased from suppliers
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: the opportunity cost of using resources owned by the firm itself, such as the entrepreneur's own capital or time, for which no direct cash payment is made

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: The accountant's definition of cost typically includes:
options: explicit costs only, that is, actual money payments made by the firm
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: explicit costs only, that is, actual money payments made by the firm

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: The economist's definition of cost, unlike the accountant's, includes:
options: both explicit costs and implicit costs (opportunity costs of self-owned resources)
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: both explicit costs and implicit costs (opportunity costs of self-owned resources)

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: Normal profit is best described as:
options: the minimum return necessary to keep an entrepreneur in a particular line of business, treated by economists as a cost of production
the same thing as economic (supernormal) profit
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: the minimum return necessary to keep an entrepreneur in a particular line of business, treated by economists as a cost of production

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: Economic (supernormal or abnormal) profit exists when:
options: total revenue equals total cost exactly
total revenue is less than total cost
a firm makes normal profit only
total revenue exceeds total cost, including both explicit and implicit costs
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: total revenue exceeds total cost, including both explicit and implicit costs

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: In the short run, the average fixed cost (AFC) curve:
options: falls continuously as output increases, since fixed cost is spread over more units
remains horizontal at all output levels
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: falls continuously as output increases, since fixed cost is spread over more units

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: The short-run average variable cost (AVC) curve is typically:
options: U-shaped, falling initially due to increasing returns, then rising due to diminishing returns
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: U-shaped, falling initially due to increasing returns, then rising due to diminishing returns

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: The short-run marginal cost (MC) curve intersects the average variable cost (AVC) and average cost (AC) curves:
options: at the point where output is zero
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: at their minimum points

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: The long-run average cost (LAC) curve is often described as:
options: an envelope curve made up of the minimum points of a series of short-run average cost curves, reflecting economies and diseconomies of scale
unrelated to short-run average cost curves
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: an envelope curve made up of the minimum points of a series of short-run average cost curves, reflecting economies and diseconomies of scale

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: The falling part of the long-run average cost curve is generally explained by:
options: rising marginal cost of the variable factor
economies of scale as the firm expands its size
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: economies of scale as the firm expands its size

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: The rising part of the long-run average cost curve beyond the minimum point is generally explained by:
options: diseconomies of scale as the firm becomes too large to manage efficiently
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: diseconomies of scale as the firm becomes too large to manage efficiently

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: In the short run, a firm will continue to produce even while making a loss, provided that:
options: price covers average variable cost and contributes something towards fixed cost
price is below average variable cost
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: price covers average variable cost and contributes something towards fixed cost

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: A profit-maximising firm under perfect competition will produce at the output level where:
options: average cost is at its minimum, regardless of price
total revenue is at its maximum, regardless of cost
marginal cost equals marginal revenue (which equals price for a competitive firm)
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: marginal cost equals marginal revenue (which equals price for a competitive firm)

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: The portion of a competitive firm's short-run marginal cost curve that lies above the average variable cost curve represents:
options: the firm's average fixed cost curve
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: the firm's short-run supply curve

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: If a firm's price falls below the minimum point of its average variable cost curve in the short run, the firm should:
options: shut down production, since it cannot even cover variable costs
increase output to reduce average cost
continue producing at a loss indefinitely
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: shut down production, since it cannot even cover variable costs

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: Given total cost data: at 5 units, TC = N300; at 6 units, TC = N340. What is the marginal cost of the 6th unit?
A firm has total fixed cost of N1,000 and produces 200 units at a total variable cost of N3,000. What is the average variable cost per unit?
Using the data in the previous question (fixed cost N1,000, variable cost N3,000, 200 units), what is the average total cost per unit?
If a firm's marginal revenue is greater than its marginal cost at the current level of output, the firm should:
options: increase output, since doing so adds more to revenue than to cost
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: increase output, since doing so adds more to revenue than to cost

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: If a firm's marginal cost is greater than its marginal revenue at the current level of output, the firm should:
options: reduce output, since the last units are costing more than they earn
shut down immediately regardless of price
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: reduce output, since the last units are costing more than they earn

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: Which of the following best distinguishes total cost from marginal cost?
options: Total cost only exists in the long run while marginal cost only exists in the short run
Marginal cost is the sum of all costs while total cost is the cost of one extra unit
Total cost is the overall cost of producing a given quantity of output, while marginal cost is the extra cost of producing one additional unit
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: Total cost is the overall cost of producing a given quantity of output, while marginal cost is the extra cost of producing one additional unit

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: In the short run, which cost remains unchanged even if a firm produces zero output?
options: Total cost, which always equals variable cost
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: Fixed cost

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: The relationship between average revenue (AR) and marginal revenue (MR) for a firm facing a downward-sloping demand curve (such as a monopolist) is that:
options: MR lies below AR at every level of output beyond the first unit, since price must fall to sell more
MR always equals AR at every output level
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: MR lies below AR at every level of output beyond the first unit, since price must fall to sell more

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: For a perfectly competitive firm facing a horizontal demand curve, the average revenue curve and marginal revenue curve:
options: are both downward sloping and never equal
coincide, that is, AR equals MR equals price at every level of output
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: coincide, that is, AR equals MR equals price at every level of output

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: A firm breaks even (earns normal profit only) when:
options: total revenue is less than total cost
total revenue exactly equals total cost, including implicit costs
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: total revenue exactly equals total cost, including implicit costs

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: Which of the following costs would an accountant typically exclude from a firm's cost calculation, but an economist would include?
options: The opportunity cost of the owner's own capital invested in the business
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: The opportunity cost of the owner's own capital invested in the business

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: If average cost is falling as output increases, marginal cost must be:
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: below average cost

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: If average cost is rising as output increases, marginal cost must be:
options: equal to average variable cost only
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: above average cost

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: Total variable cost can be obtained from average variable cost by:
options: dividing average variable cost by output
subtracting fixed cost from average variable cost
adding marginal cost to average variable cost
multiplying average variable cost by the level of output
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: multiplying average variable cost by the level of output

Theory of Costs and Revenue.text: In the long run, a firm has no fixed costs because:
options: all factors of production, including capital, become variable and can be adjusted
government abolishes fixed costs by law
Theory of Costs and Revenue.correct_answer: all factors of production, including capital, become variable and can be adjusted

Market Structures.text: Which of the following is NOT an assumption of perfect competition?
options: Large number of buyers and sellers
Market Structures.correct_answer: Product differentiation

Market Structures.text: Under perfect competition, a firm is described as a "price taker" because...
options: it has no influence on market price
it colludes with other firms to fix price
Market Structures.correct_answer: it has no influence on market price

Market Structures.text: In perfect competition, the demand curve facing an individual firm is...
Market Structures.correct_answer: perfectly elastic (horizontal)

Market Structures.text: At short-run equilibrium, a firm maximizes profit at the output where...
Market Structures.correct_answer: MC = MR

Market Structures.text: A firm operating under perfect competition earns only normal profit in the long run because...
options: free entry and exit eliminates abnormal profit
Market Structures.correct_answer: free entry and exit eliminates abnormal profit

Market Structures.text: Which of the following best describes "normal profit"?
options: The minimum reward necessary to keep a firm in an industry, included as part of cost
Profit substantially above the minimum required to keep a firm in business
Market Structures.correct_answer: The minimum reward necessary to keep a firm in an industry, included as part of cost

Market Structures.text: In the short run, a perfectly competitive firm will continue to produce even while making a loss provided that...
options: total revenue exceeds total fixed cost
total revenue exceeds total variable cost
Market Structures.correct_answer: total revenue exceeds total variable cost

Market Structures.text: The shut-down point of a firm occurs where price equals...
options: the minimum point of average variable cost
Market Structures.correct_answer: the minimum point of average variable cost

Market Structures.text: The break-even point of a firm is reached where...
options: average variable cost is at its minimum
Market Structures.correct_answer: total revenue equals total cost

Market Structures.text: Which market structure is characterized by a single seller with no close substitutes for its product?
Market Structures.correct_answer: Pure monopoly

Market Structures.text: A key barrier to entry that helps sustain a monopoly is...
Market Structures.correct_answer: patent rights and legal restrictions

Market Structures.text: A monopolist maximizes profit at the output where...
options: price is at its highest possible level
output is at its greatest possible level
Market Structures.correct_answer: MC = MR

Market Structures.text: Compared to perfect competition, a monopolist typically charges a price that is...
options: the same as under perfect competition
Market Structures.correct_answer: higher and produces less output

Market Structures.text: Price discrimination occurs when a monopolist...
options: sells the same product at different prices to different buyers or markets for reasons unrelated to cost
sells different products at the same price
sells below cost to all consumers
Market Structures.correct_answer: sells the same product at different prices to different buyers or markets for reasons unrelated to cost

Market Structures.text: For price discrimination to be effective, the monopolist must be able to...
options: sell in a single market only
produce a homogeneous product with no branding
prevent resale between markets and separate markets with different elasticities of demand
operate under conditions of free entry
Market Structures.correct_answer: prevent resale between markets and separate markets with different elasticities of demand

Market Structures.text: In third-degree price discrimination, the monopolist charges a higher price in the market where demand is...
Market Structures.correct_answer: less elastic (more inelastic)

Market Structures.text: Which of the following is an example of price discrimination?
options: Two different shops charging different prices for different goods
A firm raising all prices due to inflation
A firm charging one uniform price to all customers
A cinema charging students less than adults for the same film
Market Structures.correct_answer: A cinema charging students less than adults for the same film

Market Structures.text: Monopolistic competition is characterized by...
Market Structures.correct_answer: many sellers producing differentiated products

Market Structures.text: Under monopolistic competition, firms compete mainly through...
Market Structures.correct_answer: product differentiation, branding, and advertising

Market Structures.text: In the long run under monopolistic competition, firms earn...
options: normal profit, because free entry competes away abnormal profit
Market Structures.correct_answer: normal profit, because free entry competes away abnormal profit

Market Structures.text: Oligopoly is a market structure dominated by...
options: a few large firms that are interdependent in their decisions
Market Structures.correct_answer: a few large firms that are interdependent in their decisions

Market Structures.text: The kinked demand curve model is used to explain...
Market Structures.correct_answer: price stability (rigidity) in oligopoly

Market Structures.text: Collusion among oligopolists to fix prices or output is known as...
Market Structures.correct_answer: a cartel

Market Structures.text: Which of the following is a non-price competition strategy commonly used in oligopoly?
options: Setting price equal to marginal cost
Market Structures.correct_answer: Advertising and product quality improvement

Market Structures.text: A firm's average fixed cost curve is shaped like...
options: a rectangular hyperbola, falling continuously as output rises
Market Structures.correct_answer: a rectangular hyperbola, falling continuously as output rises

Market Structures.text: If a firm's total revenue is less than its total variable cost, the firm should, in the short run...
options: continue producing in the short run
Market Structures.correct_answer: shut down immediately

Market Structures.text: Which of the following best defines "supernormal (abnormal) profit"?
options: Profit in excess of normal profit
Market Structures.correct_answer: Profit in excess of normal profit

Market Structures.text: One key characteristic distinguishing perfect competition from monopolistic competition is...
options: product homogeneity in perfect competition versus product differentiation in monopolistic competition
presence of advertising in perfect competition
a single seller in monopolistic competition
Market Structures.correct_answer: product homogeneity in perfect competition versus product differentiation in monopolistic competition

Market Structures.text: In perfect competition, in the long run, price equals...
options: marginal cost only, without reference to average cost
minimum average cost, which also equals marginal cost
Market Structures.correct_answer: minimum average cost, which also equals marginal cost

Market Structures.text: Which of the following is a feature of pure monopoly?
options: The firm is a price maker
There is free entry and exit
Market Structures.correct_answer: The firm is a price maker

Market Structures.text: A natural monopoly arises typically because...
options: high fixed costs and economies of scale make it efficient for a single firm to serve the market
Market Structures.correct_answer: high fixed costs and economies of scale make it efficient for a single firm to serve the market

Market Structures.text: If price is below average variable cost, a firm's loss-minimizing decision in the short run is to...
options: set price equal to marginal revenue
Market Structures.correct_answer: shut down production

Market Structures.text: Duopoly refers to a market structure with...
Market Structures.correct_answer: exactly two sellers

Market Structures.text: Which of the following market structures has the greatest number of firms with the least market power per firm?
Market Structures.correct_answer: Perfect competition

Market Structures.text: The "MC = MR" rule for profit maximization applies to...
options: all market structures, including perfect competition and monopoly
Market Structures.correct_answer: all market structures, including perfect competition and monopoly

Market Structures.text: Under first-degree (perfect) price discrimination, the monopolist charges...
options: the same price to all consumers
each consumer the maximum price they are willing to pay
a uniform price below marginal cost
Market Structures.correct_answer: each consumer the maximum price they are willing to pay

Market Structures.text: A firm's break-even chart plots...
options: marginal cost against average fixed cost
total revenue and total cost against the level of output
Market Structures.correct_answer: total revenue and total cost against the level of output

Market Structures.text: Which of the following is TRUE of long-run equilibrium in perfect competition?
options: Firms earn normal profit only, where price equals marginal cost equals minimum average cost
Firms operate below the shut-down point
Market Structures.correct_answer: Firms earn normal profit only, where price equals marginal cost equals minimum average cost

Market Structures.text: One disadvantage of monopoly to consumers is that it may lead to...
Market Structures.correct_answer: higher prices and restricted output

Market Structures.text: In monopolistic competition, excess capacity in the long run refers to the fact that firms produce...
options: at the minimum point of the average cost curve
less than the output that minimizes average cost
Market Structures.correct_answer: less than the output that minimizes average cost

Market Structures.text: Which of the following best distinguishes oligopoly from monopolistic competition?
options: Oligopoly has many firms while monopolistic competition has few
Monopolistic competition has higher barriers to entry than oligopoly
Oligopoly firms are mutually interdependent in their decisions, whereas monopolistic competition firms are not
Market Structures.correct_answer: Oligopoly firms are mutually interdependent in their decisions, whereas monopolistic competition firms are not

Market Structures.text: A price war among oligopolists is most likely to result from...
options: breakdown of a cartel agreement or competitive undercutting among firms
Market Structures.correct_answer: breakdown of a cartel agreement or competitive undercutting among firms

Market Structures.text: Which of the following is an example of discriminating monopoly practice in real life?
options: A bakery selling all loaves at the same price
A farmer selling maize at the uniform market price
An electricity company charging industrial and residential users different tariffs for the same service
A tailor charging a fixed price to everyone
Market Structures.correct_answer: An electricity company charging industrial and residential users different tariffs for the same service

Market Structures.text: At the shut-down point, a firm is indifferent between producing and not producing because...
options: total revenue equals total fixed cost
the loss from producing equals total fixed cost, which is the same loss incurred from not producing at all
Market Structures.correct_answer: the loss from producing equals total fixed cost, which is the same loss incurred from not producing at all

National Income.text: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is defined as...
options: the total value of goods produced by a country's citizens both at home and abroad
the total value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given period
the total value of a country's exports only
the total value of goods produced by a country's citizens abroad only
National Income.correct_answer: the total value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given period

National Income.text: GNP differs from GDP in that GNP includes...
options: net income earned by citizens abroad, added to GDP, while excluding income earned by foreigners domestically (i.e., GDP + net factor income from abroad)
National Income.correct_answer: net income earned by citizens abroad, added to GDP, while excluding income earned by foreigners domestically (i.e., GDP + net factor income from abroad)

National Income.text: Net National Product (NNP) is obtained by...
National Income.correct_answer: subtracting depreciation (capital consumption) from GNP

National Income.text: National Income (NI) is best defined as...
options: total value of imports minus exports
total government revenue in a fiscal year
the total money value of all final goods and services produced by the normal residents of a country in a given year, usually measured as NNP at factor cost
total value of money in circulation
National Income.correct_answer: the total money value of all final goods and services produced by the normal residents of a country in a given year, usually measured as NNP at factor cost

National Income.text: Which method of measuring national income sums the value added at each stage of production?
National Income.correct_answer: output (product) method

National Income.text: The income method of measuring national income sums...
options: all factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, and profit) earned in producing goods and services
National Income.correct_answer: all factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, and profit) earned in producing goods and services

National Income.text: The expenditure method measures national income by summing...
options: consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports (C + I + G + (X − M))
value added at each stage of production only
National Income.correct_answer: consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports (C + I + G + (X − M))

National Income.text: To avoid double counting in the output method, economists use the concept of...
National Income.correct_answer: value added

National Income.text: Which of the following is a problem encountered in measuring national income in developing countries?
options: too much automation of statistical data
the existence of a large subsistence/non-monetized sector
National Income.correct_answer: the existence of a large subsistence/non-monetized sector

National Income.text: Transfer payments (e.g., pensions, unemployment benefits) are excluded from national income because...
options: they are too small in value to matter
they do not represent payment for current production of goods and services
National Income.correct_answer: they do not represent payment for current production of goods and services

National Income.text: Which of the following would NOT be included when calculating this year's GDP?
options: the sale of a used (second-hand) car
a new car produced this year
wages paid to factory workers this year
National Income.correct_answer: the sale of a used (second-hand) car

National Income.text: National income statistics are useful mainly for...
options: comparing standards of living and economic growth over time and between countries
National Income.correct_answer: comparing standards of living and economic growth over time and between countries

National Income.text: One limitation of using national income statistics to measure welfare is that...
options: they are always calculated in foreign currency
they do not account for income distribution and non-market activities
they cannot be compared over time
National Income.correct_answer: they do not account for income distribution and non-market activities

National Income.text: The circular flow of income in a two-sector economy involves flows between...
options: firms and the foreign sector only
government and the foreign sector only
National Income.correct_answer: households and firms

National Income.text: In the three-sector circular flow model, which sector is added to households and firms?
National Income.correct_answer: government

National Income.text: In the circular flow model, injections into the income stream include...
National Income.correct_answer: investment, government spending, and exports

National Income.text: Withdrawals (leakages) from the circular flow of income include...
National Income.correct_answer: savings, taxes, and imports

National Income.text: Consumption expenditure refers to...
options: spending by firms on capital goods
spending by households on goods and services for current use
National Income.correct_answer: spending by households on goods and services for current use

National Income.text: Investment, in the macroeconomic sense, refers to...
options: expenditure on capital goods such as machinery, buildings, and inventories
buying shares on the stock exchange
depositing money in a savings account
National Income.correct_answer: expenditure on capital goods such as machinery, buildings, and inventories

National Income.text: Savings can be defined as...
options: total income earned in a year
that part of income not spent on consumption
National Income.correct_answer: that part of income not spent on consumption

National Income.text: The marginal propensity to consume (MPC) is defined as...
options: the change in income divided by the change in consumption
the change in consumption divided by the change in income
total consumption divided by total income
National Income.correct_answer: the change in consumption divided by the change in income

National Income.text: If MPC = 0.8, then the marginal propensity to save (MPS) equals...
The simple Keynesian multiplier is calculated as...
If MPC = 0.75, the value of the multiplier is...
If the multiplier is 5 and investment increases by ₦2 million, national income will rise by...
National Income.correct_answer: ₦10 million

National Income.text: The multiplier effect describes how...
options: prices always fall as output rises
government spending must always equal taxation
an initial change in spending leads to a larger final change in national income
National Income.correct_answer: an initial change in spending leads to a larger final change in national income

National Income.text: In a simple closed economy without government, equilibrium national income occurs where...
National Income.correct_answer: planned savings equal planned investment

National Income.text: In the theory of income determination, aggregate demand equals aggregate supply at the point of...
National Income.correct_answer: equilibrium national income

National Income.text: Which of the following would cause an upward shift of the consumption function?
options: an increase in consumer confidence, raising autonomous consumption at each level of income
an increase in the savings rate
National Income.correct_answer: an increase in consumer confidence, raising autonomous consumption at each level of income

National Income.text: Autonomous consumption refers to consumption that occurs...
options: only when income is very high
National Income.correct_answer: even when income is zero

National Income.text: GDP at market prices differs from GDP at factor cost because market prices include...
National Income.correct_answer: indirect taxes, and exclude subsidies
